title: Vector spaces, loosened
question: What happens to a basis when the scalars are not a field?
hook: A basis is easy to find in a vector space, but swap the field for a looser ring and some modules have none.
idea: A free module is a module that has a basis, and while every vector space is one, modules over looser rings need not be.

beats.prompt: A finitely generated module over the integers is known to be torsion-free. What can you say about it?

choices.label: It need not be free; torsion-free is a weaker idea.
choices.feedback: Torsion-free modules do form a broader class in general, but for finitely generated modules over the integers the properties line up.

choices.label: It is also free, projective and flat.
It cannot have a basis.
choices.feedback: A free module is exactly one that has a basis, and here the module is free.

beats.explain: For a finitely generated module over a principal ideal domain such as the integers, free, projective, flat and torsion-free are equivalent.

beats.prompt: Match each kind of module to what defines it.
pairs: Has a linearly independent generating set
A direct summand of a free module
Tensoring with it preserves exact sequences
beats.explain: Free modules have a basis, and projective and flat modules are larger classes to which many statements about free modules extend.

beats.prompt: Sort each module by whether it is guaranteed to be free.
items: A direct sum of free modules
An infinite cartesian product of free modules
beats.explain: Vector spaces, a ring over itself and direct sums of free modules are free, while infinite products generally are not.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong. Which one?
steps: A vector space has a basis.
A module with a basis is a free module.
So every vector space is a free module.
So every module over every ring is free too.
beats.explain: Vector spaces live over fields; if the coefficient ring is not a division ring, there exist non-free modules.
